newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia hints at reconsidering closure of radio.
newsitem.headline: Serbia hints at reconsidering closure of radio.

text.p: An independent Belgrade radio station shut down by Serbian authorities appealed for international support on Wednesday amid signs the government might reconsider its move.
Radio B-92 was knocked off the air on Tuesday by authorities trying to halt reporting on a wave of daily street demonstrations against President Slobodan Milosevic.
But after the closure prompted severe criticism from Western powers, the authorities issued a statement which left the door open to restoring the radio station's signal.

The director of state Radio Television Serbia (RTS), Dragoljub Milanovic, instructed technicians "to determine the circumstances and reasons for halting of broadcasts of radio station B-92", said the statement carried by state media.
The public would be informed of the findings, the statement said.
Radio B-92 staff said the announcement indicated that outcry over the closure had forced the authorities to reconsider.

"It is a clear signal that they are affected by international media reporting about this and by international condemnation and that they might reconsider the decision," radio director Sasa Mirkovic said.
"This is their mildest option so they can test public opinion to determine what might happen tomorrow," he said.
After the authorities closed Radio B-92, a student station in Belgrade and Radio Boom in the town of Pozarevac, Serbia had only two remaining independent radio stations in smaller towns.
Radio B-92's transmitter was switched off on Tuesday and federal authorities sent a letter saying it was operating illegally.
The radio staff issued a statement calling on countries attending this week's London conference on the Bosnia peace process to push for the station's "right to broadcast".
"The case of B-92 is not an isolated one," the statement said.
Another independent station in neighbouring Croatia has also come under severe pressure, the statement said.
Lasting peace in Bosnia could only be achieved if the world upheld democractic reform in the two most powerful countries in the region, Croatia and Bosnia.

"The stability which is needed to implement a reconstruction programme in Bosnia successfully can only be reached if all human rights are respected and the cause of democracy is served," the radio said.
Saying it had strongly opposed Milosevic's "war-mongering policy", Radio B-92 said: "The truth was a victim of war and apparently is also a victim of peace".
Radio staff said they had been flooded with messages of support from abroad by fax, telephone and e-mail.
At the end of an opposition demonstration on Wednesday, supporters stood below the windows of opposition headquarters in Belgrade to listen to B-92 news over loudspeakers.
From its cramped offices in the city centre, Radio B-92 has struggled to provide an alternative source of information to state television and radio since it was founded in 1989.
